title: Ang 250–262: Bavan Akhri
tomorrow: why is Simran's own name on the Sukhmani's first page?

cards: Simran's little cousin Gurleen is on the living-room floor with alphabet cards, shouting each letter at the ceiling. Ura. Aira.
Eeri. Simran is next to her with the driver's handbook, memorizing road signs, which are just another alphabet. Then Gurleen holds up a card and asks: but what's this one for?
Simran opens her mouth, and has nothing. Guru Arjan wrote a whole poem for that question. It's called Bavan Akhri, fifty-two letters, and it starts on Ang 250.

teach.b: Before a single letter, the poem opens with a salok, in paraphrase: the Divine Guru is mother, the Divine Guru is father, the Divine Guru is master and the transcendent Lord.
The Divine Guru is the friend who destroys ignorance, kin and brother; the giver who teaches the Name. So the first thing the alphabet poem tells you is who the teacher is.
Then the letters come, stanza by stanza, each opened by a letter, and each letter turned into a lesson about the Name. It's an acrostic, the oldest kind of classroom trick: A is for apple.
Except here every letter points past itself, toward the One. That's the answer to Gurleen's question. A letter on its own is a shape.
With a teacher, it becomes a door. And notice the order. Not letters first, then a teacher to explain them.
The teacher first, as mother and father, as a friend who clears the dark, and only then the alphabet.
The Guru is the one who makes them mean something.
A road sign works the same way: a red octagon is just a shape until somebody teaches you it means stop.

how: Bavan Akhri is read in the Granth's order and sung as kirtan; its opening salok, naming the Guru as mother, father, friend and giver of the Name, is also sung on its own.

throw out the textbook; the Guru teaches without any letters.

games.why: before a single letter, the salok names the teacher: mother, father, friend who destroys ignorance. then every letter points past itself.

practice: Write the first letter of your name on any scrap of paper, slowly, as if you were learning it. Next to it, write one word that starts with that letter and names something you're grateful for.
Look at the two together while you breathe: a letter, and what it points to.
